vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus sits in the office with his shoulders drawn inward, fingers fidgeting with the fabric of his jeans. He's a lean man with dark circles under his eyes that suggest many nights of broken sleep. His wife, Priya, sits beside him—she's the one who insisted he come in. Marcus works as a senior editor at a mid-sized publishing house, a job he'd felt genuinely proud of until about eight months ago.

The incident happened on a Tuesday evening. Marcus had been leaving work late, around 9 PM, walking toward the parking garage. Two police officers approached him near his car, claiming they were investigating break-ins in the area. Marcus, trying to be cooperative, answered their questions. But something shifted quickly. One officer became aggressive, demanding to know what he was doing there, suggesting he matched a description. Marcus felt his chest tighten as the officer's tone escalated. Within minutes, he was against his car, being patted down, while the other officer called in his information. Marcus kept thinking about his mother's warnings, stories his father had told him about being treated differently. The search lasted maybe five minutes, but it felt endless. Eventually, they apologized—said it was a mistake, the description didn't match after all—and let him go.

Now, eight months later, Marcus can't drive to work anymore. He takes the subway, though even that triggers him. Whenever he sees a police officer on the platform, his heart races, his palms sweat, and he finds himself counting exits. At work, his concentration has deteriorated significantly. He's an editor—his job requires careful attention to detail, the ability to lose himself in text for hours—but he can't sustain focus anymore. He reads the same paragraph four, five, six times. His boss has noticed. They've been patient, but Marcus knows the comments are coming.

The hypervigilance has become exhausting. He scans every space he enters, noting exits, potential threats. When Priya suggests they go out to dinner, Marcus feels a spike of anxiety. What if they get pulled over? What if something happens? He's started avoiding situations where he might encounter law enforcement. He didn't attend his cousin's wedding two months ago because it was in a neighborhood he didn't know, and the thought of driving there, of being vulnerable and unfamiliar with the area, felt unbearable.

At night, Marcus lies awake replaying the moment the officer's hand touched his shoulder. He can feel the pressure of the car against his back. He remembers the shame, the powerlessness, the sudden awareness that his identity—his brown skin, his appearance—had made him suspicious in a way that felt deeply personal and utterly beyond his control. Some nights he wakes in a cold sweat, his shirt soaked through, his heart pounding as though the encounter is happening in real time.

Priya has been supportive, but Marcus can see the toll it's taking on her. She wants her husband back—the one who was excited about editing, who made plans, who wasn't afraid all the time. Marcus wants that version of himself back too, but the world feels fundamentally different now. He's more aware of how visible he is, how his presence can be read as threat rather than simply as a person going about his day. That awareness hasn't faded. If anything, it's deepened, spreading like a stain through his daily life.
